[SUMMARY]  
**Clinical Diagnosis:** Lichen Sclerosus (LS), biopsy-confirmed  
**Key Findings:**  
- Chronic (12-month) vulvar pruritus and progressive dyspareunia  
- Absence of classic visible lesions (e.g., porcelain-white plaques, fissuring)—*clinical–histologic dissociation* observed  
- Histopathology: Hyperkeratosis, epidermal atrophy (thinning), loss of rete ridges, and dermal sclerosis — pathognomonic for LS  

**Management Implications:**  
- First-line therapy: High-potency topical corticosteroid (e.g., clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment), applied daily for 6–12 weeks, then tapered to maintenance dosing (e.g., twice weekly) indefinitely

- Consider referral to dermatology or gynecologic oncology for specialist management and surveillance  
- Rule out comorbidities (e.g., autoimmune thyroid disease, vitiligo, alopecia areata) given LS associations

- Chronic (12-month) vulvar pruritus and progressive dyspareunia — hallmark symptomatic presentation of LS  
- Clinical–histologic dissociation explicitly noted: absence of classic visible lesions (porcelain-white plaques, fissuring) despite definitive histology  
- Management plan specifies first-line high-potency topical corticosteroid (clobetasol 0.05%), consistent with standard-of-care for LS  
- Counseling points include disease chronicity, low-but-elevated SCC risk, and need for long-term surveillance — all specific to LS

- No information on menopausal status (relevant for atrophy context and treatment response)  
- No details on skin color/phototype (clinical–histologic dissociation is more common in darker skin tones, but not specified)  
- No report of extragenital involvement (e.g., perianal, upper thighs, arms), which would support systemic LS phenotype  
- No serologic data (e.g., thyroid antibodies, antinuclear antibody) to assess for associated autoimmune conditions — though not required for diagnosis  

[ESCALATION]  
None. There is no finding suggestive of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (e.g., non-healing ulcer, nodule, induration, bleeding), lichen planus (no violaceous papules, Wickham striae, or erosive oral involvement described), or autoimmune blistering disease (no bullae, Nikolsky sign, or mucosal involvement). [DIAGNOSIS]  
Lichen sclerosus
